glossaryTerms.definition: Italy's national centre for recognising foreign academic qualifications. CIMEA doesn't issue the Declaration of Value itself, but its Statement of Comparability, issued digitally through its Diplòme service, is now accepted by many universities as an alternative route to the same recognition.

A document only an Italian embassy or consulate can issue, translating your degree into terms an Italian university or employer understands: what it's equivalent to, and whether it qualifies you for the programme you're applying to.

The Ministry-run portal every non-EU applicant must pre-enrol through before a consulate will process a study visa. You register, list up to three university and programme choices in order of preference, and upload your academic documents there — this has to be complete before the visa interview, not alongside it.

Your residence permit — the document that lets you stay in Italy past 90 days, separate from the visa that got you in. You apply for it within 8 working days of arrival via a kit from the post office, then attend a fingerprinting appointment at the Questura before the card itself is issued.

The local police headquarters responsible for immigration matters, including your residence permit appointment. It's where your fingerprints are taken and where you eventually collect the permit card once it's printed.
The residence permit application pack, collected free from an Italian post office, that starts the permesso di soggiorno process. It bundles the forms plus a payment slip for the required fees.

Italy's 16-character personal tax ID. Nothing official works without it — not university enrolment, not a bank account, not a rental contract. You can request it during Universitaly pre-enrolment or, once in Italy, at the local Agenzia delle Entrate office.

The 'equivalent ISEE' used to calculate what an international student actually pays in tuition, based on family income and assets declared from abroad. Filed incorrectly, a public university defaults you to its highest fee bracket — and you can't be considered for a DSU regional scholarship at all without it.

Each Italian region runs its own agency — DSU Toscana, ERSU Piemonte, LazioDisco and so on — administering need-based scholarships: full tuition exemption, a cash stipend, and often subsidised housing and meals, decided by your ISEE Parificato and your university's own merit rules.

A scholarship many universities apply automatically once you meet their published academic bar — no separate form in most cases. A handful of universities do run a distinct application and notify successful students directly, usually in spring.

A standardised online entrance test run by CISIA, a consortium of Italian universities. Most Bachelor's programmes with limited places require it, and even open-enrolment courses often use it to check you're prepared rather than to filter you out.
The dedicated entrance exam for the English-taught Medicine and Dentistry programmes at Italian universities — a separate test from TOLC, and considerably more competitive.
Italy's first-cycle degree, roughly equivalent to a Bachelor's — three years and 180 credits (CFU) under the Bologna 3+2 system most of Europe follows.

The second-cycle degree, equivalent to a Master's — two further years and 120 credits, taken after a Laurea Triennale or an accepted foreign equivalent. A handful of fields, Medicine, Architecture and Law among them, skip the split entirely and run as a single five- or six-year cycle.
Italy's version of ECTS credits — the unit every Italian degree is measured in. A Bachelor's runs 180 CFU, a Master's 120.
The visa required for any stay in Italy longer than 90 days — every full degree programme falls under this category. It's an entry document only; you convert it into a residence permit after arrival.
Covers stays of up to 90 days across the whole Schengen area, and is only relevant to short courses or exchanges — a full Bachelor's or Master's always needs a Type D instead.

A short-stay registration filed at the Questura within 8 days of entering Italy from within the Schengen area — not the permesso di soggiorno, and skipped automatically if you're staying somewhere that registers guests itself, like a hotel.
An Italian revenue stamp, bought at a tobacconist, required on certain official applications. A residence permit application typically needs two €16 stamps.

A letter, usually from your previous institution, confirming your degree was taught in English. Most Italian universities accept this in place of an IELTS score for admission, though a handful still ask for it regardless, and it doesn't help with the visa's own language-course rules if you're separately taking an Italian course.

The verification chain Pakistani academic documents must pass through before they can be legalised for use abroad: board or university verification, then IBCC (matric/intermediate certificates) or HEC (degrees), then Pakistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, then the Italian embassy. Each stage checks the stamp from the one before it, which is why doing them out of order means starting again.

FBR is Pakistan's Federal Board of Revenue; an NTN (National Tax Number) is the registration it issues. Consulates read a sponsor's NTN and tax filing history as evidence that declared income is real, not just a large balance that appeared shortly before the application.
A short, programme-specific essay explaining why you're applying to that exact course, not a template letter. Most universities read it as the clearest signal of whether an application is genuine.

A CV format standardised across the EU, structured so admissions staff who don't know your country's education system can still read it quickly. Several Italian universities ask for it specifically rather than accepting any CV layout.

A mandatory condition of the study visa: cover of at least €30,000 for medical treatment and repatriation, valid across Italy and the Schengen area for the whole visa period. You can hold private cover, or once resident, register with Italy's national health service (SSN) instead.

The amount you must show you can cover for a year in Italy, set by the Ministry of University and Research and revised periodically; for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 intakes it is €10,179.85. It can be shown through your own bank statements, a sponsor's, a scholarship letter, or a combination.

Non-EU students on a study residence permit can work up to 20 hours a week, capped at 1,040 hours a year overall — a fixed annual cap, not something you can save up and spend all at once over a summer.

Universities in Italy set admission thresholds in a CGPA scale, while Pakistani transcripts report percentages — so every programme's stated requirement needs converting before you can tell if you actually qualify, which is why we check it programme by programme rather than by a single rule of thumb.

A certificate your institution issues confirming you're currently enrolled and expected to complete your qualification by a given date, used when your final degree or high school certificate isn't issued yet at application time.

faqUpdates.how-much-money-do-i-need-to-show: For the 2026/27 and 2027/28 intakes, the Ministry-set threshold is €10,179.85 for the year, shown through your own bank statements, a sponsor's, a scholarship letter, or a mix of these. What matters more than hitting the number exactly is that it is consistent with your sponsor's tax record — a strong balance with no matching income history reads as arranged funds, not real support.

newFaqs.question: Do I need a TOLC or IMAT score?
newFaqs.answer: Only for specific programmes. Most Bachelor's courses with limited places use TOLC as an entrance test, sometimes to rank applicants, sometimes just to confirm you're prepared. Medicine and Dentistry taught in English use IMAT instead, which is considerably more competitive. Check the specific programme in our university and programme directory — not every course requires one.

newFaqs.question: What's the difference between a Type C and Type D visa?
newFaqs.answer: A Type C (Schengen) visa only covers stays up to 90 days, so it never applies to a full degree. Every Bachelor's or Master's programme requires a Type D national visa, which you convert into a residence permit after you land.

newFaqs.question: Is health insurance actually required, or just recommended?
newFaqs.answer: Required. Your visa application needs proof of cover for at least €30,000 in medical costs and repatriation, valid in Italy and the rest of Schengen for your full visa period. Private cover works for the visa stage; once you're resident, most students switch to the national health service instead.

newFaqs.question: What's the actual difference between a Laurea Triennale and a Laurea Magistrale?
newFaqs.answer: A Laurea Triennale is Italy's Bachelor's — three years, 180 credits. A Laurea Magistrale is the Master's that follows it — two more years, 120 credits. A few fields, including Medicine, Architecture and Law, skip the split and run as one five- or six-year single-cycle degree instead.

newFaqs.question: Can I bring my family with me?
newFaqs.answer: It's possible through family reunification once you hold a residence permit of at least one year, but it adds its own income and housing requirements on top of your student file. Tell us early if this applies to you — it changes how we plan your financial documentation.

blogPosts.title: CIMEA and the Declaration of Value: what actually happens to your degree
blogPosts.excerpt: Two different processes get confused constantly: the CIMEA statement and the embassy's Declaration of Value. Here's what each one actually does.

body.p: Almost every applicant asks us the same question eventually: does my degree need CIMEA, or a Declaration of Value, or both? The confusion is fair, since the two processes solve the same problem from different directions.

body.h: What a Declaration of Value is
body.p: A Dichiarazione di Valore can only be issued by an Italian embassy or consulate in the country where your qualification was awarded. It states what your degree is equivalent to inside the Italian system, and Italian institutions rely on it to decide whether you meet a programme's entry bar.

CIMEA itself does not issue the Declaration of Value. What it offers instead is a digital alternative: a Statement of Comparability, delivered through its Diplòme platform, that a growing number of universities now accept in place of the traditional embassy document. It's often faster, but not every university recognises it yet, so we check before recommending which route to take.

Whichever route applies to you, this step depends on Pakistani attestation being finished first: your HEC or IBCC stamps have to exist before an embassy or CIMEA can act on them. Starting attestation late is the single most common reason this step becomes a bottleneck.

blogPosts.title: ISEE Parificato: how Italy actually decides your tuition fee
blogPosts.excerpt: Public tuition in Italy isn't a flat number — it's calculated from a document most applicants have never heard of until they need one.

body.p: Public Italian universities rarely charge a single flat tuition figure. Instead, most set fees on a sliding scale tied to household income, and for a foreign applicant, that scale runs off a specific calculation: the ISEE Parificato.

ISEE Parificato is the 'equivalent ISEE' — a version of Italy's standard means-testing certificate, adapted for families whose income and assets sit outside Italy. It converts your family's foreign financial picture into the same scale Italian universities already use for their own students.

Get it right, and a lower-income household can end up paying only the fixed regional tax, often in the range of a few hundred euros a year, instead of the top tuition bracket. Skip it, or file it incorrectly, and the university has no basis to place you anywhere except the highest band by default.

It isn't only about tuition. A correctly filed ISEE Parificato is also the document that determines whether you can even be considered for a DSU or regional scholarship — without it, an application to your region's study-grant agency won't be evaluated at all.

blogPosts.title: The permesso di soggiorno, step by step: kit, Questura, and the card
blogPosts.excerpt: One postal kit, one fingerprint appointment, one wait. Here's exactly what each stage of the residence permit process involves.

body.p: The permesso di soggiorno is not the same document as your visa, and treating it as an afterthought is how people end up out of status without realising it. Here is the sequence, stage by stage.

Within 8 working days of arriving, collect the application kit, sometimes called the Kit Giallo, free from a designated post office. It contains the forms plus a payment slip covering the postal handling fee and the electronic permit charge.

Complete the kit and hand it back at the post office with copies of your passport, visa, enrolment letter, health insurance and financial documents. You'll receive a receipt confirming your application is logged, plus a date for your Questura appointment.

At the appointment, your fingerprints are taken for the permit's biometric chip. Bring the originals of everything you submitted in copy — the receipt alone doesn't guarantee you'll be waved through without them.

Processing the card itself typically takes anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on the local Questura's backlog. You'll get an SMS when it's ready for collection — until then, the postal receipt is your proof of legal stay.

blogPosts.title: TOLC and IMAT: do you actually need an entrance exam?
blogPosts.excerpt: Not every Italian programme requires a test — but the ones that do treat it as a hard filter, not a formality.

body.p: Whether you need an entrance exam in Italy depends entirely on the specific programme, which is exactly why we check this programme by programme rather than giving a blanket answer.

TOLC is a standardised online test run by CISIA, a consortium most Italian universities belong to. Programmes with capped enrolment often use it to rank applicants competitively; open-enrolment programmes sometimes still require it, but only to confirm you're prepared, not to filter you out.

Medicine and Dentistry taught in English run on a separate, more competitive test: the International Medical Admissions Test. It's a single annual sitting, and seats are limited nationally, so preparation timelines look very different from a standard TOLC-based application.

body.h: What this means for your shortlist
body.p: A programme's entrance-test requirement can rule it in or out of a realistic shortlist just as much as your CGPA can. We flag this at the eligibility-review stage, before you spend time on a motivation letter for a course you'd need months of test preparation to actually get into.

blogPosts.title: Italy's degree system, and where a Pakistani transcript fits into it
blogPosts.excerpt: Laurea Triennale, Laurea Magistrale, CFU credits — the vocabulary is unfamiliar, but the underlying structure maps cleanly onto what you already have.

body.p: Italy runs on the Bologna 3+2 structure most of Europe shares, but the local names for each stage throw off a lot of first-time applicants.

The first-cycle degree, equivalent to a Bachelor's: three years, 180 CFU credits. Admission requires a recognised secondary-school qualification — for Pakistani students, that means your matric and intermediate results, attested through the usual HEC/IBCC chain.
The second-cycle degree, equivalent to a Master's: two further years, 120 CFU credits, open to anyone holding a Laurea Triennale or an accepted foreign Bachelor's.
Medicine and Surgery, Veterinary Medicine, Dentistry, Pharmacy, Architecture and Law don't split into 3+2 at all — they run as one continuous five- or six-year Laurea Magistrale a Ciclo Unico.

CFU is Italy's local unit for the same idea as ECTS credits elsewhere in Europe — it's what admissions offices actually compare when assessing whether a foreign qualification lines up with a given year of an Italian programme.
